The Rule is opposed by the concerned Commissioner of Taxes (respondent No.3) by filing affidavit-in-opposition contending, inter alia, that since the petitioner admittedly received the said amount of Taka 8 crore from the developer company and invested the same in FDRs as if it was his own money, the concerned tax authorities, namely the Inspecting Joint Commissioner of Taxes and the Commissioner of Taxes, correctly held that the said amount should be treated as income from capital gains making the petitioner liable to pay tax thereon in view of the provisions under section 31 of the said Ordinance. The further contention of the respondent is that in view of the provisions under section 120 of the said Ordinance, the Inspecting Joint Commissioner of Taxes had ample power to revise any error found in the orders passed by the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes, and, as such" in the instant case, the respondent No.2 committed no illegality in revising the assessment of the petitioner in exercise of such power. 

 4. Mr MA Noor, learned advocate appearing for the petitioner, at the very outset, has drawn our attention to two judgments of this Court, namely Reliance Insurance vs Commissioner of Taxes 65 DLR 426 and unreported judgment of this Court in IT Reference Application No. 319 of 2013 (Mrs Nilufar Sattar vs The Commissioner of Taxes). Referring to the first cited case of Reliance Insurance, Mr Noor submits that this Court in the said case has elaborately discussed the power and ambit under section 120 read with sub-section (3) of section 82BB of the said Ordinance and finally held that in presence of sub-section (3) of section 82BB empowering the NBR to select certain numbers of assessments done under Universal Self Assessment Scheme for audit, the Inspecting Joint Commissioner of Taxes is immune from invoking the jurisdiction under section 120. Referring to the subsequent decision, namely the unreported case of Nilufar Sattar vs the Commissioner of Taxes (IT Reference Application No. 319 of 2013).learned advocate argues that the said case was decided almost on the similar facts as the present one and their Lordships in the said case held that the 'signing money' or 'earnest money' as received by the owners of land upon signing of development agreements with a developer are nothing but the part of sale proceeds to be received by the said developers on behalf of the owners of land after sale of the developers portion of flats to the prospective purchasers. Thus, according to him, since at the time of sale of those flats by the developers through registration, taxes will be deducted in view of the provisions under section 53H, being tax deductible at source, such deduction of tax at the time of registration for sale of those flats on behalf of the owner of land is deemed to be the final discharge of tax liability in view of the provisions under section 82C (1)(q) of the said Ordinance. Mr Noor then submits that this being the correct legal position as decided by this Court in so far as receiving the 'signing money' or 'earnest money' by a land owner in a joint venture development agreement is concerned, both the Inspecting Joint Commissioner of Taxes and the Commissioner of Taxes, by their impugned orders, acted without jurisdiction out of their sheer misconception of relevant laws. Thus, he continues, this Court should interfere in such gross illegality touching the jurisdiction of those officers under the said Ordinance. 

 6. The admitted position in this case is that the petitioner was initially assessed under Universal Self Declaration Scheme in view of the provisions under section 82BB of the said Ordinance and, accordingly, he was given a receipt thereto making it a deemed assessment for the concerned assessment year. Now the question is whether the Inspecting Joint Commissioner of Taxes (IJCT) can revise such an assessment under section 120 of the said Ordinance. It appears from mere reading of the provisions under section 120 that- the IJ CT has the authority to call for any records from the DCT in respect of any proceeding before him under this Ordinance if the UCT considers that any order passed. in the said proceedings is erroneous and such error caused prejudice to the interest of the revenue, and, upon examination, he may pass such order thereon according to the circumstances of the case and such order may include the order of enhancing or modifying the assessment or cancellation of the assessment and directing a fresh assessment to be made. From the above reading, it appears that, the pre-requisite for exercising such power under section 120 is the existence of an order in a proceeding under the Ordinance before the DCT. However, in a case of assessment under Universal Self Assessment Scheme in view of the provisions under section 82BB at the relevant time, there was no such order to be passed by the DCT. Though sub-section (1) of section '82BB provides that a receipt issued by the DCT shall be deemed to be an order of assessment for the said assessment year, what is tangible before the UCT for revision is not an order, but a receipt. Therefore, in a case where assessment is completed' under Universal Self Assessment Scheme, the only provision for reopening the said assessment at the relevant time was sub-section (3) of section 82BB through selection for audit. This view as regards the jurisdiction of the UCT under section 120 read with section 82BB as adopted by a Division Bench this Court in the aforesaid Reliance Insurance case is thus a correct decision of law and this Court finds no reason to deviate from the same. This being so, we find substance in the submissions of Mr Noor in that the IJCT did not have any jurisdiction under section 120 to revise the assessment of the petitioner completed under Self Assessment Scheme. 

 7. Now, coming to the next point, namely the issue of 'signing money'. It has now become prevailing practice in the real estate business in Bangladesh that an owner, while entering into a Joint Venture Agreement with the properly developer for development of his land into an apartment project, receives a certain amount of money which is widely known as 'signing money'. This issue of 'signing money' and whether it can be treated as capital gains for taxing purposes in view of the provisions under section 31 read with section 2 (15), was taken up by this Court in another case on a similar set of facts like the present one, namely in the unreported case of Nilufar Sattar vs The Commissioner of Taxes (IT Reference Application No. 319 of 2013). The observation of the author Judge (Mr Justice AFM Abdur Rahman) in that case on the issue of signing money is so pertinent in the instant case that the relevant portion of that decision is quoted below: 

 8. In deciding the above case, their Lordships basically held that the 'signing money', 'earnest money' or 'advance money', whatever may it be called, when a certain amount is received by the owner of land at the time of signing a development agreement is in fact an advance payment of sale proceeds of those flats which will be sold by the developer, by virtue of a registered power of attorney, to the prospective purchasers of flats. Therefore, for example, when the owner of the land is paid Taka Two crore as 'signing money', 'earnest money' or 'advance money' and the owner gives power, under the development agreement and registered power of attorney, to the developer to sell the developer's portion of the flats (usually 50% or 40% of the total flats) to the prospective purchasers of the same, the said amount of Two crore is adjusted against the total sale proceeds upon such sale of flats. Thus, if the developer, after completion of the project, sells ten apartment flats under his portion to the prospective buyers and gets 20 crores as total sale proceeds, he will in fact be receiving Taka 18 crores because of the fact that he had already paid two crores in advance to the land owner. However, when the said ten apartment flats are to be mandatorily registered for such sale on behalf of the owner of land, the person registering the said deeds of sale is required to make sure that certain prescribed rate of tax is deducted at source from the sale proceeds in view of the provisions under section 53H of the said Ordinance. In such scenario, it may appear that the developer is in fact receiving Taka 18 crore after adjustment of Taka 2 crore signing money already paid to the land owner, the tax is being assessed on the entire sale proceeds, namely on Taka 20 crores. This is the reason why the Legislature substituted the provision of 82C and inserted 53H vide Finance Act, 2011 making provision for deeming discharge of tax liability by such deduction. ]f the contention of the tax authorities is to the effect that since the 'advance money', 'signing money'or 'earnest money'; as received by the land owner, is used by the land owner as if it is his own money even some times by investing the same in the FDRs and, as such, the same should be taxed as capital gains, there will certainly be double taxation on the same amount in as much as that the said amount of earnest money is to be merged in the total sale proceeds of the flats to be sold by the developer to the prospective buyers in accordance with development agreement. Therefore, the very concept of 'signing money' or 'earnest money' as received by the petitioner in this case has been misconceived by the tax authorities and, as such, the same has been regarded as capital gains without jurisdiction. Thus, this Court is of the view that, the entire exercise of powers by the customs authority, in so far as this 'signing money' or 'earnest money' is concerned, either under section 120 or under section 121 A are without jurisdiction and, as such, this Court under writ jurisdiction can interfere into the same. 

 9. Regard being had to the above facts and circumstances of the case as well as the relevant provisions of law discussed above, we are of the view that since the tax authorities have exercised jurisdiction beyond its power as given under section 120 read with 82BB as well as section 121 A of the said Ordinance, the Rule has substance and, as such, the same should be made absolute.
